newsitem.title: INDIA: Demand spurs India Basmati rice exports, prices.
newsitem.headline: Demand spurs India Basmati rice exports, prices.

text.p: Robust demand from Europe, the Middle East and the United States has boosted exports of Indian Basmati rice and pushed up its price, industry officials and traders said on Wednesday.
"The demand for Indian Basmati is very strong from Europe, the Middle East and America," Rashmi Bhimjayani, a leading Bombay foodgrains exporter, told Reuters.
India exported 392,000 tonnes of Basmati rice in 1995/96 (April-March), industry officials said.
"Probably Basmati exports this year may surpass last year's figures," Bhimjayani said, adding that the industry did not have an agreed export forecast for 1996/97.

Bhimjayani said Basmati exports to Europe surged to about 100,000 tonnes in 1995/96 from around 35,000 tonnes in 1994/95. In the current financial year ending on March 31, Basmati exports to Europe are projected at 125,000 to 150,000 tonnes, he said.
He said the United States, which until last year had imported no more than 15,000-20,000 tonnes a year of Indian Basmati, was expected to buy around 35,000-40,000 tonnes in 1996/97.
"Indian Basmati is getting very popular in the restaurants in Western countries," Bhimjayani said.
Industry officials said Indian Basmati prices were sharply higher compared with last year due mainly to stronger demand from the Middle East and Europe.
Bhimjayani said Kuwait and Oman together were also expected to buy around 50,000 tonnes of Basmati.

Traders said Indian parboiled Basmati was currently priced at around $780 to $800 per tonne FOB compared with $620 at the same time last year. Raw Basmati was quoted at around $900 to $1,000 per tonne against $725 to $775 a year ago.
"Demand mainly from the Middle East and Europe had pushed up Basmati rice prices this year," Anil Adlakha, executive director of the All India Rice Exporters Association, told Reuters.
Bhimjayani said a surge in demand from the Middle East and a rise in domestic demand by about 15 percent had spurred prices.
"Saudi Arabia had sufficient carryover stocks last year, but this year they don't have sufficient stocks," Bhimjayani said. "So we feel the sales to Saudi Arabia will be good."
Bhimjayani said the 1996/97 (July-June) Basmati crop was expected to be the same size as in 1995/96, when India produced nearly 600,000 tonnes of Basmati, according to trade sources.
He said farmers had reduced Basmati acreage this season by about 10 to 20 percent because prices had declined last year.
"But the production is expected to be the same compared to last year as the yield is expected to go up to 1,000 kg per hectare against 750 kg last year," Bhimjayani said.
